title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
body:
Cryptography chosen to survive a large quantum computer. The threat is specific and it is not
"quantum computers are fast": it is two algorithms.

| Algorithm | Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Shor** (1994) | factoring and discrete log in **polynomial** time | [[RSA]], [[Diffie-Hellman]], [[ElGamal]], [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] all die completely |
| **Grover** (1996) | unstructured search in $O(\sqrt{N})$ | halves the effective key length of a symmetric cipher |

The asymmetry is the whole story. **Grover is survivable by doubling the key**: [[AES]]-256 retains
128 bits of security, and a 512-bit [[Cryptographic Hash Function|hash]] retains 256. Shor is not
survivable by any parameter choice, because it is a polynomial-time algorithm for exactly the
[[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] and factoring assumptions the whole of
[[Public Key Cryptography]] rests on. **Every public-key scheme in this course is broken by a
sufficiently large quantum computer; no symmetric one is.**

Shor works by turning the problem into finding the *period* of a function, and periods are what
quantum interference measures well. The core of it is the quantum Fourier transform, which is the
[[Discrete Fourier Transform]] from [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] realised as a circuit. That is
a genuine connection rather than a coincidence: the [[Roots of Unity]] and the [[Cyclic Group]]
structure that make the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] work are what make Shor work.

**"Harvest now, decrypt later"** is why this is urgent rather than academic. An adversary can record
encrypted traffic today and decrypt it when the hardware arrives, so anything that must stay secret
for twenty years is already at risk. Migration also takes a decade, which is why NIST standardised
replacements in 2024: **ML-KEM** (Kyber) for key agreement and **ML-DSA** (Dilithium) for
[[Digital Signature|signatures]], both lattice based.

The candidate hard problems are chosen for having no known quantum algorithm:

- **Lattices**, the leading family. The shortest-vector problem in a high-dimensional lattice, a
  discrete grid of points in a [[Vector Space]] generated by integer combinations of basis vectors.
  Its hardness is *not* a period-finding problem, so Shor does not apply, and unusually it has a
  worst-case to average-case reduction, which is a guarantee the
  [[Cryptanalysis|classical assumptions]] lack.
- **Hash based** signatures, whose security rests only on the hash function and is therefore the
  most conservative option available. Stateful and with limited signature counts.
- **Code based** (McEliece), resting on the hardness of decoding a general linear code. Forty-five
  years unbroken, with megabyte-sized public keys. The same [[Error Correcting Code]] material from
  [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] read as a hardness assumption instead of a repair mechanism.

Deployments are **hybrid**: run the classical and post-quantum key exchange together and combine
both secrets, so the connection is secure if *either* holds. The new schemes are young and nobody
wants to bet a decade of traffic on them alone.
